newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, Palestinians close in on Hebron deal.
newsitem.headline: Israel, Palestinians close in on Hebron deal.

text.p: Months of painstaking U.S. efforts to broker a deal between Israel and the Palestinians on the West Bank town of Hebron appeared to be drawing close to fruition, with an agreement possible this year.

Israeli and Palestinian negotiating teams pressed ahead in late-night meetings on Thursday with drafting the text of a deal under which Israel would hand over 80 percent of Hebron, home to 400 Jews and 100,000 Arabs, to Palestinian self-rule.

In Washington, U.S. U.S. Middle East peace envoy Dennis Ross briefed President Bill Clinton on the negotiations, which last week appeared close to collapse, and a White House spokeswoman said Clinton was "pleased by the progress."
The top-level U.S. review of the talks came amid reports that Palestinian President Yasser Arafat expected to seal a Hebron accord with Israel next week.

Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai met Jibril Rajoub, Palestinian preventive security chief in the West Bank, in Tel Aviv to work out details of security arrangements for the volatile West Bank town, an Israeli source said.
East Jerusalem lawmaker Ziyad Abu Ziyad told Reuters that Arafat said a deal was on the near horizon when he briefed Palestinian legislators in Ramallah on the negotiations.
"If the Israelis go ahead with their promises and the plans which were planned, maybe it will be possible to conclude an agreement on the 30th and the 31st (of December)," Abu Ziyad said.
Other Palestinians officials confirmed Arafat's remarks, which reinforced a senior Israeli official's estimate that a deal could be wrapped up before the end of the year.
Israeli security sources have said the promised troop redeployment in Hebron could be completed within days of the signing of an accord.

Abu Ziyad said Arafat also expressed caution. "President Arafat said that maybe there would be no agreement at all...This (Israeli) government has been cunning and manoeuvring and trying to run away and ignore their commitments," he said.
Tensions remained high in the Hebron itself after a firebomb was thrown near a Jewish enclave in the heart of the town.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu wants security guarantees for the Jewish settlers in Hebron, a town sacred to Moslems and Jews and a hotbed of militancy for both.
Netanyahu insisted to far-right sceptics that the pending Hebron deal was far superior to an accord signed by the left-leaning government which he ousted in May.
"We will act in every place and at every time necessary to defend Jews," he told a meeting of the ultranationalist Moledet party where he was greeted with jeers.
Most of Netanyahu's 18 cabinet ministers were expected to back the deal although some, including hawkish former general Ariel Sharon, have openly criticised it as dangerous for the Jews of Hebron.

Hebron, taken by Israel with the rest of the West Bank in the 1967 Middle East war, is the last Palestinian town due for self-rule under a 1995 peace deal. Israel's security fears have delayed its transfer.

A troop withdrawal from Hebron is seen as the key to further Israeli-Palestinian peace moves. Arabs view a pullout, promised by Israel's former government, as an acid test of Netanyahu's intentions toward the Middle East peace process as a whole.
